{{short description|Canadian statistician}}
'''Priscilla E. (Cindy) Greenwood''' (born 1937)<ref>Birth year from [http://id.loc.gov/authorities/names/n84116297.html Library of Congress catalog entry], retrieved 2018-12-07.</ref> is a Canadian [[mathematician]] who is a [[professor emeritus]] of mathematics at the [[University of British Columbia]].<ref>[http://www.math.ubc.ca/People/people.shtml?group=Emeritus Faculty directory] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181209124228/http://www.math.ubc.ca/People/people.shtml?group=Emeritus |date=2018-12-09 }}, UBC Mathematics, retrieved 2015-08-16.</ref> She is known for her research in [[probability theory]].<ref name="queen">{{citation|title=Priscilla Greenwood: Queen of Probability|arxiv=0712.3459|first1=I. V.|last1=Evstigneev|first2=N. H.|last2=Bingham|author2-link=Nicholas Bingham|journal=Stochastics|year=2008|volume=80|issue=2–3|pages=103–113|doi=10.1080/17442500801886176|s2cid=115156354}}. Reprinted in ''Stochastics: A Festschrift for Priscilla Greenwood'', IMS Lecture Note Series 57A, Institute of Mathematical Statistics.</ref>

==Education and career==
Greenwood graduated from [[Duke University]] with a B.A. in 1959. She began her graduate studies in [[operations research]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], where she became exposed to probability theory through a course on [[stochastic process]]es offered in 1960 by [[Henry McKean]].<ref name="queen"/> Soon afterwards, she switched to the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]], where she completed her Ph.D. in 1963 under the supervision of Joshua Chover.<ref name="queen"/><ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=8409}}</ref> She taught for two years at [[North Carolina College]] before moving to the University of British Columbia in 1966. She has also been associated with [[Arizona State University]], as a visiting professor from 2000 to 2003 and since 2004 as a research professor.<ref name="queen"/>

==Research==
Greenwood's research in the 1970s concerned [[Brownian motion]], [[Lévy process]]es, and [[Wiener–Hopf factorization]]. During this method she developed the theory of the martintote, a process similar to a [[Martingale (probability theory)|martingale]] used to study asymptotic properties of processes.<ref name="queen"/>

In the 1980s Greenwood began working with [[Ed Perkins]] on [[nonstandard analysis]], which they used to study [[Local time (mathematics)|local time]] and [[Excursion probability|excursions]]. In this timeframe she also began working on set-indexed processes, a topic that would lead her to the theory of [[random field]]s, and on [[semimartingale]]s. She traveled to Russia, and wrote a monograph on [[chi-squared test]]s with Mikhail Nikulin.<ref name="queen"/>

In 1990 she and Igor Evstigneev wrote a second monograph, on random fields. Her research in this period also concerned [[Measure-preserving dynamical system|metric entropy]] and [[Efficiency (statistics)|asymptotic efficiency]]. She began her work in [[biostatistics]], involving studies of different mammalian populations, and led a major study on statistical estimation near critical points of a parameter.<ref name="queen"/>

Beginning in 2000, at Arizona State, she studied [[pink noise]] and [[stochastic resonance]], which she applied to epidemic models in biostatistics as well as to the firing patterns of neurons.<ref name="queen"/>

==Awards and honours==
Greenwood was elected as a fellow of the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]] in 1985. She won the [[Krieger–Nelson Prize]] of the [[Canadian Mathematical Society]] in 2002.<ref name="queen"/><ref name="Krieger–Nelson lecturer Priscilla Greenwood">{{cite web | title=The 8th Krieger-Nelson Prize Lecture | url=https://cms.math.ca/wp-content/uploads/awards/citations/kn2002.pdf | access-date=2024-03-02}}</ref>
